lis-aqueduto.s: Almost three hundred years ago, Lisbon did not have enough clean water. So people built the Águas Livres Aqueduct, which means “Free Waters”. It is a long stone bridge, but cars do not drive on it. Inside, water runs along a stone channel. The aqueduct strides across the valley on tall arches, like a giant on stilts, and the biggest arch is higher than a twenty-storey building. Even in the big earthquake of 1755, the aqueduct stayed standing.

lis-telecabine.s: In the Parque das Nações, little cabins hang from a cable and travel along the River Tagus. This cable car was built in 1998 for a big world fair. The cabins have glass windows, and from above you can see the river, the ships and the very long Vasco da Gama Bridge. The cabins glide through the air slowly, like little clouds. The ride lasts only about ten minutes, but it feels like flying.

lis-calcada.s: The pavements of Lisbon are made of small stones, white and black. Craftsmen lay them by hand, stone by stone, like a mosaic, and this kind of pavement is called calçada. In Rossio Square, the stones make black and white waves. As you walk on them, it feels as if the ground is rocking like the deck of a ship! Similar waves were later laid in Brazil, on the famous Copacabana beach.

lis-coches.s: In the Belém area of Lisbon there is a Coach Museum. Queen Amélie, the wife of King Carlos, opened it in 1905. Here stand real royal carriages: golden, with carved figures and soft seats. Several horses pulled one carriage. It is one of the biggest collections of carriages in the world, and you feel that Cinderella might step out of one any minute!

lis-c-popugai.s: Wild green parrots live in the parks of Lisbon. They have bright green feathers and a red beak. Once, these birds lived only in hot countries, but now whole flocks fly screeching over the trees of Lisbon, because it is warm here. You can hear them from far away, because they call loudly and clearly. Look up, and you will see a flash of green between the branches.

lis-c-kukly.s: Lisbon has a puppet museum. Marionettes are puppets on strings, worked from above. In the halls stand puppets from Portugal, Asia, Africa and other countries. Next to them sit little puppets that you wear on your hand, such as the cheerful Dom Roberto, the favourite of street shows. The Portuguese have shown such puppet shows for a long time, and children always laugh when the puppet bows or waves.

lis-c-treska.s: People in Lisbon love a fish called bacalhau. It is cod that is first salted and then dried. On the stall this fish lies as hard as a board and hardly smells. Before cooking, it is soaked in water for a long time, and it becomes soft again. They say the Portuguese have so many bacalhau recipes that there is one for every day of the year: they fry the fish, bake it, boil it with potatoes and make fluffy fishcakes from it.
a: Soak it in water for a long time
Put it straight into ice cream

lis-c-nauka-dlya-detej.s: In Lisbon, on the bank of the River Tagus, stands a science museum called the Pavilion of Knowledge. Almost everything there may be touched. Children press buttons, turn levers, build with big pieces and see how physics works. You can test how water flows or how a shadow is made. They leave tired but happy, and the mums and dads play too.

us-ny-subway.s: The New York subway opened in 1904, more than a hundred years ago. Today it has over four hundred stations, and the trains run all day and all night, even in the middle of the night. At some stations, musicians sit playing guitars and violins. You are waiting for your train, and suddenly a little band is playing on the platform. Waiting is not boring at all.
a: Only when the sun is shining

us-ny-statenferry.s: In New York you can sail on the sea without paying a penny. The orange ferry goes from Manhattan to Staten Island, and the ride is free. It takes about twenty-five minutes. On the way, the ferry passes close to the Statue of Liberty, and the skyscrapers get smaller behind you. Seagulls fly along after the boat, the wind blows your hair about, and all the passengers, big and small, take photos of the city from the water.

us-dc-cherry.s: Every spring, thousands of cherry trees blossom in Washington, and the whole city turns pink and white. The trees came from Japan: in 1912 that country gave Washington about three thousand trees. The first two young trees were planted by the lake by the President’s wife and a lady visiting from Japan. Some of those very trees still flower today. With cherry blossom everywhere, it looks as if the city is covered in candyfloss.

us-sf-cablecar.s: Little wooden cars travel up and down the steep hills of San Francisco. They have no motor on the roof. Under the street, a long steel cable always runs along, and the car grabs it with a special grip and off it goes. The first cable car started in 1873. The driver pulls a lever, a bell rings, and the car climbs up a hill or rolls down it, while passengers stand on the steps.

us-sf-sealions.s: Sea lions live near Pier 39 in San Francisco. At the end of 1989, one came swimming in, then dozens more joined it, and by the start of the next year there were more than three hundred. They lie on wooden rafts by the boat harbour, push each other, bark loudly and are not the least bit afraid of people. The biggest ones are grown-up males, and they weigh up to four hundred kilograms.
a: On wooden rafts by the boat harbour
On the roof of a tram
On the benches in the park

us-fl-apollo.s: In Florida, at Cape Canaveral, there is a spaceport, and next to it is the Kennedy Space Center. On 16 July 1969, Apollo 11 took off from here with three astronauts. You could see their Saturn rocket from far away: it was almost a hundred and ten metres tall, like a house with more than thirty floors. Then people walked on the Moon for the very first time. The rocket’s launch could be heard for many kilometres around.
a: From a bridge in New York

us-fl-manatee.s: Off the coast of Florida swim gentle giants called manatees. People call them sea cows because they chew grass, only underwater grass: seaweed and sea grasses. A manatee is huge and weighs several hundred kilograms, but it is very calm. It swims slowly, and every few minutes it comes up to the surface to take a breath. In winter, when the water gets cold, manatees gather in warm springs and rivers to keep warm.

us-hi-kilauea.s: In Hawaii there is a volcano called Kilauea. Hawaiians say that the goddess of fire, Pele, lives in its crater. When the volcano wakes up, fountains of fire shoot out, and red-hot lava creeps down to the ocean. When it reaches the cold water, it hardens and breaks into tiny pieces. These pieces make black sand. On a beach like this, for example Punaluʻu, green sea turtles love to lie in the sun.

us-b-edison.s: Thomas Edison wanted to make a light bulb that would burn for a long time. Inside the glass bulb you need a very thin glowing thread. Edison and his helpers tried many different materials. In 1879, a burnt cotton thread glowed for more than thirteen hours. Then they tried bamboo, and that bulb burned for more than a thousand hours. So evenings became brighter, and homework by lamplight became easier.

us-b-popcorn.s: Why does a corn kernel jump in a hot pan and turn into a white fluffy cloud? Inside its hard shell it has a tiny drop of water. The heat turns the water into steam, the steam pushes from the inside, and suddenly the shell bursts: pop! Native Americans were eating popcorn many thousands of years ago. Today people love to eat it at the cinema. But not every kind of corn can pop. You need a special kind for popcorn.

old-first-hands.s: In caves all over the world, there are handprints that are many thousands of years old. One cave in Argentina is even called the Cave of the Hands. How were they made? A person pressed a hand to the rock and blew paint from their mouth through a tube made from a bone. The paint sprayed out, and under the hand a clean patch was left, the shape of a hand. Some of the hands are tiny, so little children took part in this art too!
a: They blew paint around the hand
They dipped the hand in honey
They drew it with a chocolate pencil

old-first-mammoth-house.s: In Ukraine, scientists dug up strange round houses. Their walls were built from mammoth bones and tusks! They were made about 18,000 years ago, when it was very cold, in the Ice Age. The bones were piled up like bricks, and animal skins were probably stretched over the top. Inside, people lit a fire, and it was warm. A house made of a mammoth, what an idea! But there were hardly any trees on the cold plains, and bones lay everywhere.

old-egypt-pyramid.s: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu. At first it was about 146 metres tall. It was made from around 2,300,000 blocks of stone! For more than 3,800 years it was the tallest building on Earth, and nobody could build higher. The record was only broken by a cathedral in England, finished in the Middle Ages. Just think: for 3,800 years, a pile of stones held the record!

old-egypt-cats.s: In Ancient Egypt, people loved cats very much. Cats caught mice in the barns, so the grain stayed safe. There was even a goddess with a cat’s head called Bastet. Egyptians often made cats out of clay and painted them on walls. When a pet cat died, the family was sad, and the Greek writer Herodotus said they even shaved off their eyebrows. Cats were wrapped up carefully, just like mummies. Lots of cat mummies have been found.
a: They caught mice and kept the grain safe
They could swim in the Nile on their backs

old-gr-olympia.s: The story says that the first Olympic Games were held in Greece about 2,800 years ago. They took place in a spot called Olympia, and not every year, but once every four years. Runners, wrestlers and discus throwers came from all the Greek cities. There were no gold medals back then! The winner got a crown of olive twigs on his head. For a Greek this was the greatest honour, and at home he was welcomed like a hero.
a: A gold medal on a ribbon

old-rm-teplyj-pol.s: Romans did not freeze in winter, not even in rich houses and baths. Their floors stood on low brick pillars, and under the floor a fire burned in a furnace. Hot air flowed through the empty space under the floor and through pipes in the walls. This system was called a hypocaust. So floor heating is not new: it was invented more than 2,000 years ago. But somebody had to look after the furnace by hand.

old-china-kites.s: Kites were invented in China more than two thousand years ago. Back then they were made from light silk and thin bamboo sticks, because paper came later. Kites were not only toys: they were part of festivals, and big kites were painted with dragons and birds. Today people fly kites on every continent. But the very first ones flew over Chinese fields, tied to a long silk string.

old-knights-armour.s: Many people think a knight in armour could hardly move. In fact, a full suit of armour weighed about twenty to twenty-five kilos, like a child at school. But it was made to fit the body, so the weight was spread out and did not sit on the shoulders. Armourers built it from lots of plates, so a knight could bend his arms and legs and even get on his horse by himself. The parts moved on rivets and little straps.
a: From one solid piece of stone

old-vik-longship.s: The Vikings sailed in long, narrow ships. Some had a carved dragon’s head at the front. The ship’s bottom was shallow, so it could go not only on the sea but also up small rivers. And if land blocked the way, the Vikings pulled the ship onto the shore and dragged it over logs to the next river. The boat was walking on land! There was one big sail, and when there was no wind, they took the oars.
a: They dragged the ship over the land on logs
They waited for the river to come to them
They took the ship apart and carried it in rucksacks

old-rus-onfim.s: About 750 years ago, a boy called Onfim lived in the city of Novgorod. He was six or seven and went to school. Onfim learned his letters and scratched them on pieces of birch bark. He drew too: a knight on a horse beating his enemy, and a scary beast. Under the beast he wrote: “I am a beast.” These bits of bark lay in the ground for almost seven centuries, until archaeologists found them. Now we can see how a boy from long ago loved to draw.
a: He learned letters and drew pictures

old-first-flute.s: More than 35,000 years ago, someone made a flute in a cave in Germany. It was carved from the wing bone of a big bird, a vulture, and it has five little holes for the fingers. The flute broke into pieces, but scientists found them and put them back together. It is about as long as a ruler, over twenty centimetres. So there was music when people still lived in caves and hunted mammoths.
a: From the bone of a big bird

old-egypt-tutankhamun.s: Pharaoh Tutankhamun became ruler when he was just a child, about nine years old. He lived around 3,300 years ago and did not rule for long. His tomb was found in 1922 by an Englishman, Howard Carter, and it was full of treasure: a golden mask, chariots, chairs, sandals. There were thousands of things! For a little boy, it was a whole room of toys and clothes that waited a very long time, until the scientists came.

old-gr-antikitera.s: In 1901, sponge divers found a sunken ship near the Greek island of Antikythera. Among the things was a lump of green bronze. Scientists found out that inside there were gears! It is a device more than 2,000 years old. It showed where the Sun and the Moon were in the sky, told people when an eclipse would come, and even counted the years until the next Olympic Games. A clock and a calendar in one box.
a: The Sun and the Moon moving, and eclipses
How many biscuits are left in the pantry

old-rm-priglashenie.s: Around the year 100, in the Roman fort of Vindolanda in the north of Britain, lived a woman called Claudia Severa. She wrote an invitation to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina for her birthday party. She wrote it in ink on a thin wooden tablet. At the end she added in her own hand: “I will wait for you, sister.” The tablet is still here today, so we can read the oldest party invitation.
a: On a card with a kitten
On a page from an exercise book

old-china-silk-thread.s: Silk is made by caterpillars called silkworms. They eat the leaves of the mulberry tree and then wrap themselves in a cocoon. The amazing part: the cocoon is made of just one single thread, hundreds of metres long! In ancient China, people learned to unwind the cocoons and weave the threads into soft, shiny cloth. The Chinese kept the secret of silk for many years, and the cloth travelled to far-away lands along the Silk Road.

old-knights-drawbridge.s: Around many castles people dug a deep ditch, called a moat, and sometimes filled it with water. A drawbridge led across the moat to the gate. In the daytime it was lowered, and carts and visitors came in. When danger came near, the guards pulled thick chains or ropes, and the bridge went up. It closed the gate like a big wooden door. It was hard to cross the moat without the bridge, so everyone in the castle felt safe.

old-vik-horns.s: You have probably seen pictures of a Viking in a helmet with big horns. But they never really had such helmets! Horns would get in the way in a cramped boat and catch on branches. A Viking helmet was plain and round, with a guard for the nose. Horned helmets were made up by artists and theatres about a hundred and fifty years ago, for fine costumes in the opera. A real Viking helmet was found in Norway. It is smooth, with no horns at all.
a: No, artists and theatres made up the horns
Yes, they scared cows with them
Yes, they carried water in the horns

old-rus-bortniki.s: In old Rus, as medieval Russia was called, honey came from wild bees. The honey hunters, called bortniki, found a thick tree with a hollow in the forest, or carved a hollow themselves. Bees moved in and made honey. The hollow could be very high up, ten metres above the ground. The bortnik climbed the tree, tied on with a rope, and took the honey carefully, so that the bees had enough for the winter. Honey was the main sweet treat, because there was no sugar then.

old-rm-termopolii.s: In the city of Pompeii there were fast-food shops on the streets, called thermopolia. They had a counter with round holes, and big pots of hot food were set into them. Not long ago, archaeologists dug up one of these shops almost whole. On the counter, ducks and a rooster are painted. Scientists think this was the menu: what is painted is what they sold. Bones left in the pots show that this is true.
a: Ducks and a rooster, like a menu

old-egypt-senet.s: The Egyptians loved to play. One of their favourite games was called senet: a board with three rows of ten squares, and playing pieces. Players took turns throwing sticks, like dice, and moved their pieces. Several senet boards were found in Tutankhamun’s tomb! But the rules were lost, and scientists still argue about how it was played. Today people play senet with made-up rules. Just think: the game is thousands of years old, and nobody knows the rules for sure!

por-lello.s: There is a bookshop in Porto called Lello. It is more than a hundred years old. In the middle of the shop, a red staircase rises up. It twists and splits in two, like a ribbon on a present. Above it shines a ceiling window of coloured glass, and the shelves are full of books right up to the top. It is one of the most beautiful bookshops in the world, and people from all over the Earth queue up to peek inside.

por-sao-bento.s: In Porto there is a train station called São Bento. When you walk into its big hall, it feels like you have stepped into a giant picture book. The walls are covered with white and blue tiles called azulejos, about twenty thousand of them! The tiles make pictures of olden times: kings and knights, and village parties. High up near the ceiling runs a colourful stripe. It shows how people travelled long ago, first in carts and later on the train.

por-clerigos.s: Above the roofs of Porto rises the Clérigos Tower, tall and thin like a pencil. An Italian architect, Nicolau Nasoni, designed it, and it was finished in 1763. At that time it was the tallest building in all of Portugal. To climb to the top, you must go up more than two hundred steps on a narrow spiral staircase. But from up there you can see the whole city: red roofs, the River Douro and boats on the water.

por-francesinha.s: In Porto people love a huge sandwich called the “francesinha”, which means “little French girl”. Inside there is bread, ham, sausage and a piece of meat. On top, it is covered with melted cheese and poured over with hot sauce, and often a fried egg sits on the very top like a little hat. You cannot pick this sandwich up with your hands. You eat it with a knife and fork. They say it was invented by a man who had lived in France for a long time and then came home to Porto.

por-a-thin-house.s: In Porto two churches, Carmo and Carmelitas, stand right next to each other. They say there was once a rule that two churches must not share a wall. So a tiny house was built between them, to keep the walls from touching. The house is so thin that you can hardly notice it: it is only about one metre wide. It has a white front and small windows, like a doll’s house. If you walk past, you may wonder how a person fits inside. But the house is real, and people really lived in it.
a: A thin house to live in
A tall tower with a clock

por-b-grape-harvest.s: In autumn, the grape harvest begins on the slopes of the Douro. The grapes are cut with scissors and carried in baskets. And then comes the funny part. The grapes are tipped into a low stone tank called a “lagar”, and people squash them with their bare feet, sometimes even to music! Some farms still do it this way today, although there are machines too. The juice comes out sweet and thick, and afterwards your feet stay purple for a long time.

por-b-iberian-wolf.s: In the mountains of northern Portugal lives the Iberian wolf. It is grey, with a dark stripe on its legs, and a little smaller than other wolves. Wolves live in families and carefully keep away from people. It is almost impossible to see them, but at night you can sometimes hear them calling to each other with howls. Wolves help keep the forest in order: they take the sick and weak animals.

por-ribeira.s: The old riverside of Porto is called Ribeira. The houses there are tall and narrow, and every one has a different colour: yellow, blue, pink, orange. They stand close together, shoulder to shoulder, like felt-tip pens in a box. Washing dries at the windows, and boats sail down on the River Douro. The old centre of Porto is so beautiful that the whole world looks after it like a treasure.

por-guimaraes.s: A cradle is a little bed for a baby. The city of Guimarães is called the cradle of Portugal, because this is where the country began. On an old city wall, big letters say: “Portugal was born here.” Above the town stands a stone castle with pointy towers. The first fort on this hill was built more than a thousand years ago.

por-braga.s: Near the city of Braga, a huge staircase leads up a high hill. It zigzags like a snake, and fountains splash on its landings. Next to it, a little funicular car goes up the hill, and since 1882 it has been moved by water! The top car is filled with water, so it gets heavier and rolls down, pulling the other car up on a cable. It is the oldest water-powered funicular in the world that still works.

por-a-douro-spain.s: The River Douro is not born in Portugal, but in the country next door, Spain. It is there too, but it is called the Duero. It flows for almost nine hundred kilometres, through fields, hills and vineyards. On the way its banks become steep, like steps for a giant. And in Porto the Douro finally reaches the ocean and flows into it. The river makes this long journey without a rest. What a tireless traveller!

por-a-tram-sea.s: Porto has tram line number one, and it is a special one. An old wooden tram leaves from the Ribeira and rolls along the River Douro. The wheels clatter softly, the seats are made of wood, and the windows are open. The further you go, the wider the river gets, until the ocean appears. The last stop is in the Foz area, where the Douro meets the sea. Passengers get off and go for a walk along the shore, to breathe the salty wind and watch the waves.
a: To the ocean, along the river
To the mountains in the north

por-a-dragon-stadium.s: The football club Porto has blue and white colours, and a dragon sits on its badge. The team’s stadium is called the “Estádio do Dragão”, which means “Dragon Stadium”. It opened in 2003 and holds about fifty thousand people. When the team plays, the stands sing songs and wave flags and scarves. On the pitch a cheerful mascot runs around. It is a dragon too, and its name is Draco. You can spot the fans in the city at once by their blue and white scarves.

por-a-henry-born.s: More than six hundred years ago, a boy called Henry was born in Porto, so people believe. He was a prince, but he liked maps and ships more than feasts. When he grew up, he gathered sailors, builders and scientists to look for new sea routes. That is why he was later nicknamed the Navigator. He hardly went on long voyages himself, but he thought up ways for ships to sail further. In Porto there is still an old house where, so the story goes, he was born.

por-a-bolhao.s: In the centre of Porto stands the old Bolhão market. In the past you could buy everything in its aisles: vegetables, fruit, fish, flowers, cheese and fresh bread. The sellers called out loudly to shoppers and told jokes. Above the rows there are tall balconies with iron railings, and below it smells of greens and the sea. The market was repaired for several years and opened again in 2022. Now it is noisy again, and very tasty. Children love to look at the bright heaps of apples and oranges.

por-b-caldo-verde.s: In the north of Portugal people love “caldo verde”, which means green soup. It is made of potatoes and a special cabbage with big leaves, cut into very, very thin strips. A spoonful of olive oil goes into the bowl, and sometimes a slice of sausage. The soup is warm, thick and tasty. People serve it at parties, and at home when it is cold and drizzling outside.

por-a-crystal-peacocks.s: Porto has a big garden around the former Crystal Palace. The palace of glass and iron was once built for an exhibition, and later it was gone, but the garden stayed. Peacocks walk calmly along the paths. They spread their huge tails like green and blue fans and call out proudly. Tall trees and flowers grow nearby, and from the edge of the garden you can see the River Douro. Children love to come here to watch the birds and play on the grass. But you must not touch the peacocks!

ru-big.s: Russia is the biggest country in the world. You could fit more than one hundred and eighty countries the size of Portugal inside it! Russia is so wide that it has eleven time zones. When children in Kaliningrad go to bed, it is already morning in Kamchatka. The children there are waking up and getting ready for nursery.

ru-transsib.s: The longest railway in the world runs through Russia. It is called the Trans-Siberian Railway. A train takes almost a week to go from Moscow to Vladivostok! Outside the window you see forests, rivers, mountains and even Lake Baikal. On the train you can sleep on a bunk, drink tea and watch the country change. In Vladivostok, right by the sea, there is a post with the number 9288. That is how many kilometres the train has travelled.

ru-baikal.s: Lake Baikal is the deepest lake in the world. Its water is so clean that you can see pebbles on the bottom, even very far down. In winter Baikal freezes, and the ice can be clear as glass. You look down at your feet and see water! Baikal is also home to the nerpa, a round seal with big dark eyes. You cannot find these seals anywhere else in the world, only in Lake Baikal.
a: An elephant in a stripy jumper

ru-geysers.s: Kamchatka is a land of volcanoes. It has many fire-breathing mountains, and some of them sometimes wake up and puff out smoke and ash. Kamchatka also has the Valley of Geysers. A geyser is a hot spring. Suddenly a fountain of boiling water and steam shoots out of it: pshhh! There are no roads to the valley, so visitors are flown there by helicopter.

ru-tiger.s: In the taiga, a thick forest in the Russian Far East, lives the Amur tiger. It is one of the biggest cats in the world. It is not afraid of snow or frost, because it has thick warm fur and a layer of fat under its skin. Every tiger has its own stripes, just like your fingerprints. That is how scientists tell tigers apart in pictures taken by cameras hidden in the forest.

ru-oymyakon.s: Oymyakon is a village in Yakutia. It is one of the coldest places on Earth where people live. In winter it can be colder than sixty degrees below zero! If you throw a cup of boiling water into the air there, it turns into a little cloud of snow at once. Yakut horses live outdoors all year. Their fur is thick and long, as warm as a fur coat. And in summer it can even get hot in Oymyakon.

ru-matryoshka.s: A matryoshka is a wooden doll with other dolls hiding inside it, each one smaller than the last. The first matryoshka was made more than a hundred years ago. It had eight dolls. The biggest was a girl holding a black rooster, and the smallest was a little baby in a blanket. This matryoshka is still kept today in a toy museum in the town of Sergiev Posad. People there still carve and paint matryoshkas.

ru-c-pelmeni.s: The word “pelmeni” comes from the Ural mountains. The Komi-Permyak people lived there, and in their language “pelnyan” means “bread ear”. Look at a pelmen: it really does look a bit like a tiny ear made of dough! In Siberia people made hundreds of them at once and put them out in the frost. The frozen pelmeni went into a sack, and a hunter took it along on his journey. Boil some water, and dinner is ready.

ru-maslenitsa.s: Maslenitsa is a merry festival to say goodbye to winter and welcome spring. For a whole week people make blini, which are thin pancakes: round, golden and hot like a little sun. They are eaten with sour cream, honey or jam. People slide down hills, dance in circles and have snowball fights. On the last day they burn a big straw doll called Maslenitsa. That is how they say goodbye to winter.

ru-d-belka-strelka.s: On 19 August 1960 two dogs, Belka and Strelka, flew into space. They travelled in a spaceship, went around the Earth 17 times and landed safely a day later. The dogs were cheerful, and people welcomed them home like heroes. Later Strelka had puppies, and one of them, called Pushinka, was given to the daughter of the American president, Caroline. People still remember Belka and Strelka today. There is even a cartoon about them.

ru-bears.s: Many big brown bears live in Kamchatka. In summer, lots of salmon swim from the sea up the rivers. The fish swim against the current and even jump over rocks and little waterfalls. The bears stand right in the river and catch them with their paws and teeth. That way they get nice and fat, so they can sleep all winter in their den.
a: To put them in a cupboard

ru-volga.s: The Volga is the longest river in Europe. It starts as a tiny stream that you can step over. Then it grows so wide that you can hardly see the other bank. Big boats sail on the Volga, and large cities stand along its banks. At the end of its long journey, the Volga flows into the Caspian Sea. People lovingly call it “Mother Volga”.

ru-elbrus.s: In the Caucasus mountains stands Elbrus, the highest mountain in Russia and in all of Europe. It is 5,642 metres tall! Elbrus has two white peaks, like the two humps of a camel. It is a sleeping volcano covered with snow and ice. Even in summer there is snow, and brave climbers go up in warm jackets and dark glasses.

ru-ustyug.s: Father Frost lives in the old town of Veliky Ustyug. His wooden house stands in the forest, not far from the town. Children from all over Russia send letters here, whole sacks of letters! Father Frost even has his own post office. He celebrates his birthday on the eighteenth of November. People say that is when the real frosts begin in Veliky Ustyug.
a: On the first of July, when it is hot

ru-kizhi.s: On Kizhi island, in the middle of Lake Onega, stands an amazing wooden church. It has twenty-two domes, round tops that look like little onions. It was built in 1714 almost without nails. The logs fit tightly together, like the pieces of a wooden building set. And the little wooden tiles on the domes shine in the sun like silver.

ru-murmansk.s: Murmansk is the biggest city north of the Arctic Circle, far in the north. In winter the polar night comes: for more than a month the sun does not show up in the sky at all. But sometimes the northern lights appear, green ribbons of light that wave like curtains in the wind. In summer it is the other way round: the sun shines all day and night and never goes to bed.
a: The sun shines even at night

ru-a-metro-dvortsy.s: The Moscow metro is not just trains. Many stations look like palaces, with marble, chandeliers and pictures made of tiny pieces of coloured glass on the ceiling. At the station called Revolution Square there are bronze statues of people. Next to them sits a bronze dog called Ingus. Passengers stroke her nose for luck, so the nose shines like gold. You can ride to get somewhere, or just ride around and look at the stations, like in a museum under the ground.
a: Her nose, which people stroke for luck

ru-b-kalan-kurily.s: The Kuril Islands are a long chain of about fifty islands between Kamchatka and Japan. In the cold waves near the shore lives the sea otter. It sleeps on its back in the water and wraps itself in seaweed so it does not drift away. The sea otter picks up shellfish from the seabed and cracks them open with a stone that it keeps in a fold of skin. Its fur is so thick that the water never reaches its body.

ru-d-chaikovsky.s: The composer Pyotr Tchaikovsky wrote the music for the ballet “The Nutcracker”. For the dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy he needed a very special sound, like little drops of glass. He brought a new instrument from Paris, the celesta. It looks like a small piano with little bells inside. People say he wanted the sound to be a surprise for the audience, so he kept it secret until the first night. In the town of Klin, near Moscow, there is a house where he wrote music. Now it is a museum.

ru-d-gagarin.s: On the 12th of April 1961, a rocket lifted off from the Baikonur space centre. Yuri Gagarin was sitting in the spaceship Vostok. Before the start he cheerfully shouted, “Poyekhali!”, which means “Let’s go!” He flew once around the whole Earth and came back. The whole flight took 108 minutes, less than two hours. From space Gagarin saw that our planet is blue, and he told the people on Earth. Today that day is called Cosmonautics Day.

sgp-a-merlion.s: By the water in Singapore stands an amazing statue. It has the head of a lion and the body of a fish, with scales and a tail. Its name is the Merlion. It is as tall as a three-storey house, and it spouts water from its mouth all day long. The fish reminds us that Singapore was once a fishing village. The lion reminds us that Singapore means “lion city”. There is also a tiny baby Merlion nearby, only two metres tall.
a: A fish body, with scales and a tail

sgp-a-supertrees.s: In the Gardens by the Bay stand the Supertrees, and they are not real trees. They are made of metal! They are between twenty-five and fifty metres tall. But real flowers and ferns climb up their trunks. Some of the tops have solar panels that collect sunlight in the daytime. In the evening the Supertrees glow in lots of colours, and a light show begins, with music. Everyone looks up and cannot look away.
a: They glow in lots of colours
They fold up their branches and go to sleep

sgp-a-jewel-changi.s: Changi Airport in Singapore has often been called one of the best airports in the world. It has a building called Jewel, and in the middle of it, inside a glass house, a huge waterfall tumbles down. It is called the Rain Vortex and it is about forty metres tall. The water pours from a hole in the roof, and a whole forest grows around it. In the evening, coloured lights shine on the waterfall. Your plane is not leaving for a long time, and you are already looking at a wonder!

sgp-b-hawker-centre.s: Singapore has hawker centres. These are huge shelters with lots of tables, and all around them are dozens of tiny kitchens. One family picks chicken rice, another a noodle soup, another little skewers, and everyone eats together at one table. In 2020 UNESCO added hawker culture to its list of the world’s special traditions, because people here share good food and eat together.
a: A shelter with tables and lots of tiny kitchens
A museum where you must not touch the food
A tower where they only make tea

sgp-b-durian.s: The durian is a big fruit covered in spikes, like a medieval club. Inside is soft yellow flesh, and many people think it tastes delicious. But the smell is so strong that it stays in a room for a long time. So in Singapore’s trains and in many hotels there are signs that say: no durians! People eat them outside, or at home where they can open a window.
a: The fruit has a very strong smell

sgp-c-night-safari.s: Singapore has a zoo that you visit after sunset. It is called the Night Safari. When it gets dark, the animals that slept all day wake up: tigers, hyenas, bats and flying squirrels. A little tram rides quietly along the path between the trees, and the lights are dim, like moonlight, so the animals are not scared. It is said to be the first zoo in the world that opens at night.
a: In the evening and at night

sgp-c-otters.s: In the bay in the middle of Singapore live smooth-coated otters. They stay in families: mum, dad and the pups. You can see them by the water. They dive for fish, warm up on the bank and call to each other with thin little voices. Their fur is short and smooth, and they have webbing between their toes, so they are very good swimmers. People stop to watch them, but you should not go close.

sgp-d-chinese-new-year.s: At the end of winter or the start of spring, Chinese New Year begins in Singapore. The streets are decorated with red lanterns, because red brings good luck. Children are given red envelopes with money inside. And in the squares, lions dance! Two dancers hide under a huge lion mask: one is the head and the other is the tail. To the beat of drums, the lion nods, jumps and “eats” green lettuce. That is for good luck too.

sgp-b-ice-cream-bread.s: On a street in Singapore, you might meet a seller with a big cool box. He takes out a slice of ice cream and puts it not in a wafer cone, but in a soft bun. Or he wraps it in bright bread: pink, yellow or green. Grown-ups and children both eat ice cream this way. On a hot day, a sweet bun with a cold filling is a real treat.

sgp-b-always-summer.s: Singapore sits almost in the middle of the Earth, near the equator. So there is no winter here. It is warm and damp all year, and rain can come in any month. It often starts after lunch. The sky goes dark, thunder rumbles and the rain drums on the roofs. People in Singapore do not mind. They hide under a shelter, and then the sun comes out again and the city sparkles.
a: It is almost on the equator, where it is always warm
A ship takes the winter away

sgp-a-mbs-ship.s: Look at the Marina Bay Sands hotel. Three tall towers stand side by side, and on top of them lies a long platform that looks like a ship. It is as if a huge ship sailed through the air and landed on three pillars! It is a whole park up high, with trees and paths. There is also a swimming pool with a view of the whole city. Only hotel guests can swim in it.

sgp-a-cloud-forest.s: In another glass dome of Gardens by the Bay lives the Cloud Forest. As soon as you step in, you see a mountain covered in green plants and orchids. And from the very top a waterfall tumbles down, right inside the building! It is about thirty-five metres high. A light mist floats around, like in the clouds, and it smells of damp leaves. You can go up the mountain in a lift and come down by a winding path.

sgp-b-four-languages.s: Singapore has four official languages: English, Chinese, Malay and Tamil. Most signs in the metro are in English, because almost everyone understands it. At school, children also learn the language of their family: some learn Chinese, others Malay, others Tamil. So a boy can chat with the lady next door in one language and with his granny at home in another.
a: The language of the people on the Moon

sgp-b-chilli-crab.s: Chilli crab is a festive dish in Singapore. A whole crab is cooked in a thick sauce of tomatoes, chilli and egg. The sauce is a little sweet, a little sour and not too spicy. You eat the crab with your hands, so there are napkins and crackers for the claws on the table. Soft buns are served with it: you dip them in the sauce and mop up every last drop.
a: You dip soft buns in it
You drink it through a bamboo straw
You spread it on a giant watermelon

sgp-b-mrt-driverless.s: Singapore has a metro called the MRT. Some of its lines run without a driver: a computer drives the train. If you stand by the very first door of the front carriage, you can look ahead through the glass, as if you were steering yourself. It is easy to pay with a travel card: you tap it on the reader at the entrance and the gate opens. You can pay on the bus with the same card.

sgp-c-jurong-birds.s: For many years Jurong Bird Park was home to birds in Singapore. Pink flamingos strolled about, and macaw parrots could repeat words. Flamingos are pink because of their food: shrimps and algae contain a colouring that tints the feathers. Flamingo chicks are grey! In 2023 Jurong closed, and the birds moved to a new park called Bird Paradise. It is in another part of the island.
a: Because of their food: shrimps and algae
They are born pink from the sun

sgp-c-penguins-sgp.s: Singapore is almost on the equator, and it is hot all year round. But penguins live in Bird Paradise! A cold house with icy water was built for them, just like the South Pole. Through the glass you can watch the penguins fly under the water like little torpedoes. There is even a dome where they swim right over the visitors’ heads. On land, penguins waddle funnily from foot to foot.
a: In a cool house with a glass wall
On the roof of a skyscraper

sgp-d-diwali.s: Diwali is an Indian festival of light. In Singapore, before it begins, the whole of Little India lights up: glowing arches and lanterns hang over the street. At home, people light small clay lamps. And by the front door they make a pattern from coloured powder or rice. It is called rangoli. People believe that kind light chases away the dark, and a pretty doorstep welcomes good luck.

sgp-b-kaya-toast.s: For breakfast, people in Singapore love kaya toast. Kaya is a soft jam made from coconut milk, eggs and sugar. Often the juice of green pandan leaves is added, and the jam turns a little green and smells lovely. Thin crunchy bread is spread with kaya and topped with a slice of cold butter. Soft-boiled eggs come with it: you pour them into a little saucer and dip the toast in.

sgp-c-sentosa-cable.s: Sentosa is an island next to Singapore. In Malay, its name means “peace and quiet”. You can get there by cable car: the cabins glide high above the harbour, ships sparkle below, and skyscrapers shine far away. Sentosa has sandy beaches with palm trees, where you can build sandcastles. The trip through the air is like a little adventure.

sp-sputnik.s: On 4 October 1957, a rocket rose into the sky and carried the world’s first satellite above the clouds. It was quite small: a shiny ball with four long antennas like whiskers. The satellite flew around the Earth and sent a signal: “beep-beep-beep”. People in many countries switched on their radios and listened to the sound of space. The satellite went around the Earth in about an hour and a half. The space age had begun.

sp-belka-strelka.s: On 19 August 1960, two dogs flew into space: Belka and Strelka. With them were mice, insects and even plants. The spaceship went around the Earth 17 times, then landed gently, and everyone came home safe and well. Belka and Strelka became famous all over the world. Later Strelka had puppies. One of them, called Pushinka, was given as a present to the family of the American President Kennedy, and lived in their home.

sp-gagarin.s: On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space. He was born in a village, and as a boy he dreamed of aeroplanes. His spaceship was called Vostok. Before the launch, Gagarin said cheerfully: “Poyekhali!”, which means “Let’s go!” He flew once around the Earth, and the whole flight lasted 108 minutes. From space he saw our planet and said it was blue. Then he came safely back to Earth.

sp-armstrong.s: On 20 July 1969, the American spacecraft Apollo 11 landed on the Moon. Neil Armstrong climbed down the ladder and said: “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” So he became the first person on the Moon. Buzz Aldrin walked in the moon dust with him. They collected rocks and set up instruments. There is no wind and no rain on the Moon, so footprints do not get wiped away. They can stay for a very long time.
a: There is no wind or rain there

sp-eda.s: Long ago, astronauts ate from tubes, like toothpaste, but tasty: soup, mash and even juice. Today they also have ordinary meals in packets. Astronauts rarely take bread, because it makes crumbs. In weightlessness, crumbs do not fall down. They float in the air and could get into eyes or machines. So astronauts eat carefully and close their packets.

sp-mks.s: The International Space Station is a huge home that flies above the Earth. Astronauts from different countries live there, taking turns. The station goes around the Earth in about an hour and a half, so in one day they see about sixteen sunrises. If the sky is clear, you can even see the station from Earth. It is a bright dot that moves quickly across the sky and does not blink. Wave to it when you see it!

sp-sun-star.s: The Sun is a star, just like the stars you see at night. It is simply the closest one to us, so it shines so brightly and keeps us warm. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth. The Sun is huge: more than a million planets like ours would fit inside it. It is a ball of very hot gas. In the daytime the bright Sun hides the other stars, and we only see the blue sky.
a: It is the closest one to us
It is the biggest star in the world

sp-mars-rovers.s: On Mars, robots on wheels are at work: Mars rovers. Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012, and Perseverance in 2021. They have cameras, arms and tools to study red rocks and dust. Perseverance also brought a little helicopter called Ingenuity. It was the first helicopter to rise into the air over another planet. It flew very low, but it was a real flight!

sp-aurora.s: In the cold far north, for example in Norway or Iceland, green and pink ribbons of light sometimes spread across the sky. They move like huge curtains. These are the northern lights. The Sun sends tiny particles towards the Earth, and high above us they bump into the air, and the air starts to glow. The lights are most often green. The best time to see them is in winter, on a dark, frosty night.

sp-meteors.s: Sometimes at night a bright streak zooms across the sky. People call it a shooting star, but it is not a star. It is a meteor: a tiny grain of dust from space flies into the Earth’s air and flashes brightly high above us. It burns up before it reaches the ground. There are especially many in August, and this shower of stars is called the Perseids. There is a kind old saying: make a wish before the streak fades!
a: A tiny grain of dust that flashed in the air

sp-skafandr.s: A spacesuit is a space outfit, like a tiny spaceship you can climb into. In space there is no air, and the temperature changes a lot. So the suit has air to breathe, and the helmet has special glass that protects the eyes from the bright Sun. Under the suit, the astronaut wears special underwear with thin tubes, and cool water flows through them. The gloves are thick, but you can still hold tools in them.

sp-nevesomost.s: When you float, there is no “up” or “down”, so astronauts sleep in sleeping bags tied to the wall. Sometimes a sleeper’s arms float in front of them. Astronauts wash in a special way, too: water in space does not run down, it gathers into little balls. So they use wet towels and damp wipes. After brushing their teeth, they can wipe the toothpaste away carefully with a wipe.
a: In sleeping bags by the wall
On the ceiling with no bag

sp-galilei.s: A long time ago, in 1609, the scientist Galileo Galilei made a telescope and looked at the sky at night. He saw mountains on the Moon! And next to Jupiter he saw four little stars. They turned out to be moons of Jupiter. Every night they stood a bit differently, which meant they were going round the planet. Galileo drew it all in his notebook and showed people. That is how looking at the sky through a telescope began.

sp-hubble.s: The Hubble telescope flies around the Earth, high above the clouds and the air. From there the stars look very sharp, because air does not get in the way. It was launched in 1990 and is named after the scientist Edwin Hubble. The telescope has taken thousands of pictures: far-away planets, clouds of dust and huge islands of stars. Hubble’s photos look like bright paintings. Many of them hang in museums and appear in books.
a: Around the Earth, high above the air

sp-halley.s: A comet is a big ball of ice and dust. When it flies close to the Sun, the ice warms up and a bright tail appears around it. The tail always points away from the Sun, like a light puff of smoke in the wind. The most famous comet is named after a scientist called Halley. It comes back to Earth about every seventy-six years. It was last seen in 1986, and it will be seen next in 2061.

sp-star-colors.s: If you look closely, stars come in different colours. Some are white, others bluish, others yellow or orange, and some are reddish. The colour tells you how hot a star is. Blue stars are the hottest, yellow ones, like our Sun, are a bit less hot, and red stars are the coolest. It is like a campfire: the hottest flame is bluish, and glowing embers are red. Try to find a reddish star in the sky!

sp-constellations.s: A long time ago, people joined stars with pretend lines, and pictures appeared. They are called constellations. There is the Lion, the Swan, the Scorpion and the Great Bear. In the Great Bear, seven bright stars make a big ladle with a handle, also called the Plough. It is easy to find in the northern sky. The stars in a constellation are really far away from each other. From Earth they just look close together.

sp-milky-way.s: Far from the city lights, on a dark night, you can see a pale stripe in the sky, as if someone spilled milk. This is the Milky Way. It is really a huge number of stars, so far away that they blur into a misty path. Our Sun and the whole Earth live in this big family of stars, which is called a galaxy. It has hundreds of billions of stars. Seen from above, the galaxy looks like a pinwheel with curly arms.
a: Our galaxy, a huge group of stars

sp-voyagers.s: Two spacecraft called Voyager set off in 1977 and are still flying. They are farther from Earth than anything else: more than twenty billion kilometres! Each one carries a golden record with recordings. On it are greetings in many languages, the sound of rain and waves, birdsong and music. It is like a message in a bottle thrown into space: maybe someone will find it one day and listen.
a: Greetings, sounds of nature and music

sp-eclipse.s: Sometimes the Moon floats in front of the Sun and covers it. This is a solar eclipse. In the daytime it suddenly gets dim, like evening, and the birds go quiet. The Moon is much smaller than the Sun, but it is also much closer to us, so it can cover the Sun completely. But remember the most important rule: never look at the Sun without protection, not even during an eclipse. You need special dark glasses, and grown-ups give them out.

uae-a-burj-khalifa.s: In Dubai stands the tallest building in the world. It is called the Burj Khalifa. It has 163 floors and is about 828 metres high. If you put football pitches end to end, you would need almost eight of them to reach that length. The building is narrow and stepped: each step rises higher than the one before, and the top seems to melt into the sky. People say the architects found the shape by looking at a desert flower.

uae-a-palm-build.s: How do you build an island in the sea? In Dubai they did it like this: sand was lifted from the bottom of the bay and poured in the right place, and big rocks were laid around it so the waves could not wash the shore away. That is how the “trunk” and sixteen “fronds” appeared. Around the whole palm they built a long breakwater shaped like a crescent moon. It shields the island from big waves, like a fence from the wind.
a: To protect the island from waves

uae-a-ski-dubai.s: In summer Dubai can be hotter than forty degrees. But inside one shopping centre there is real snow! It is called Ski Dubai. It is always cold there, white snow lies on the ground, and people go skiing, snowboarding and sledging. Special machines make the snow. You can build a snowman and throw a snowball, then step outside into the heat again. A warm jacket is handed to you right at the door.

uae-a-abra.s: You can cross Dubai Creek on an abra. It is a small wooden boat with a roof against the sun. It leaves when enough passengers have climbed in, just like a bus. The trip is short, a breeze blows on your face, and the boatman stands at the wheel. It costs very little. From the water you can see old houses and new shiny towers together. Abras have sailed here for many years.

uae-a-pearl-divers.s: A long time ago, before oil was found, Dubai lived on pearls. In summer the men sailed out on big boats into the gulf to look for pearls. They dived without any air tanks, filled a basket with shells and swam up. Not every shell has a pearl, so they had to open a great many. They sold the pearls they found to merchants, who took them to different countries.

uae-b-camel-lashes.s: The camel is made for the desert, and everything about it is clever. Its eyelashes are long and in two rows, like thick little brushes, and they keep sand out of its eyes. A camel also has a third, see-through eyelid. It covers the eye, but the camel can still see the way through it. It can close its nostrils when a sandy wind blows. And its feet are wide and soft like cushions, so they do not sink into the sand. See how well a camel is made for life in the desert?
a: To keep sand out of its eyes

uae-b-falcon-passport.s: Did you know that in the Emirates falcons have their own passports? The passport has details about the bird, and the falcon wears a little ring on its leg with a number that is also in the passport. The number tells one falcon from another. With such a passport a falcon can travel by aeroplane. The bird sits with a little hood on, so it does not get worried, and behaves calmly like a real passenger. Every airline has its own rules, but the main thing is that the bird is healthy.
a: A little ring with a number

uae-b-oryx.s: The Arabian oryx is a white antelope with two long straight horns. It lives in the desert and is used to the heat: its pale coat reflects the sunlight. An oryx’s horns are so slim that from the side they look like a single horn. Maybe that is why people once made up stories about unicorns. At one time very few oryxes were left, but people took care of them, and now they live in the wild again, in nature reserves. The oryx is a much-loved animal in the UAE.
a: From the side their horns look like one horn

uae-b-dates.s: The date palm is the best-known tree of the Emirates. It grows in the heat and loves the sun. Every year heavy bunches of golden-brown fruit ripen on the palm. These are dates. There are hundreds of kinds: soft, sweet, crunchy and dark. People eat them fresh and dried, put them in sweets and offer them to guests. In the Emirates there are date festivals where people bring the most beautiful bunches. And you can eat dates, skin and all!

uae-a-miracle-garden.s: A huge garden has grown in the desert: the Miracle Garden. Millions of flowers bloom there. Flowers make up not only flower beds but also arches, hearts, little houses and big figures. The flowers are watered drop by drop to save water. The garden opens when it is not too hot outside, because in summer it would be hard for the flowers and for people. You walk along the paths, and all around is a carpet of every colour of the rainbow.
